title: SCADA
promise: One page, every screen it is opened on.

hero.h1: Every screen of the plant, from one database.
hero.dek: Synoptics, faceplates, alarms, trends and the record, drawn once and served on the wall, the desk and the phone. And the line's own edge keeps serving them when the centre cannot.

The operator's pages in plant order, the page itself drawn live beside the tree, not a thumbnail.
Live values, the state of every machine and the alarm pressure on a page before it is opened.
A press on a writable signal that is attributed, timestamped, and refused in the database when the person may not.
A panel that opens on one line's home page and cannot be navigated away.

sections.title: One page, every screen it is opened on.
cols: The operator's screens are drawn once and served everywhere, from the wall panel to a phone, with nothing installed and nothing licensed per screen. Values, states, alarms and commands sit on the same page, in the language the person reading it chose.
A page is never redrawn for a second screen size: the wall panel, the desk and the phone all serve the same page.

sections.title: Machines and their documents
Every machine carries its own door, and its documents.

screen.chrome: the machine's door · Beverage Line 7 · the transfer pump
screen.caption: the machine's own door on a running line: its state, its readings, its own alarms, the causes its type carries, and its buttons

items.text: One door on the machine: its values, a small trend, its own alarms, its causes, its commands and its documents.
The machine's state, its readings, and how far each one can be trusted.
The machine's own bits, and separately what the alarm system recorded against it, never one posing as the other.

items.lead: The small trend inside the door
items.text: That machine's own readings over a short window, on the raw values, so a spike is still a spike.
The mechanical, electrical and process causes for that kind of machine, and one line naming what the alarm hides.
Start or stop without leaving the machine: two-step confirm, then a press attributed, timestamped and refused when the person may not.
The sheet opens over the page with the others beside it, nothing to search for and nothing to download first.
That machine's full page opens, in the same window.

sections.title: Put the paper in once. It opens at the machine.

screen.chrome: the editor · Beverage Line 7 · the document library
screen.caption: the line's document library: what is in it, which pages carry each one, and the press that swaps a revision

items.text: The drawings, the datasheets and the procedures that came with the machines, put in once by an engineer with design rights on the line.
Everyone who can open the page the machine sits on sees it; the file stays in the plant's private store, handed out one view at a time.

items.lead: A new revision, no page redrawn
items.text: Replace the file in the library and every machine that carries it shows the new one.
The library names every page still carrying a document, and counts them, before it lets go.
Copy the line and its documents copy with it; carry the line to the next plant as one file and the documents ride inside it.

screens.caption: the datasheet opened from the machine's own door, with the other documents beside it
nothing is removed blind: the library names the pages that still carry it

sections.title: Every machine carries its own door, and its documents.
cols: An operator who presses a pump on the page gets the machine itself: what it is doing now, what it has been doing, what the alarm system has recorded against it, and the buttons that move it. Behind the same door sits the plant's own paper, put into the line once and opened at the machine that needs it.

The fault light on the machine and the alarms under it are two different things: a pump can sit with its fault bit clear and three unanswered alarms in the journal, so the door shows both, separately.

One line, one document library: the drawings, the datasheets and the procedures that came with its machines. An engineer puts a file in once, and it opens at the machine, for everyone who can open the page that machine sits on.
The paper is part of the line: it is one press from the pump, and it goes wherever the line goes.

sections.title: Alarms
An alarm is an event with a record.

screen.caption: the alarm console under a flood: the rate against its target, what is standing, what is shelved

items.text: Signal, limit, how long it must hold, how urgent; the edge beside the machine starts judging it within seconds, with no deploy step and no restart.

items.lead: Prioritised alarms, rate and standing count
items.text: The board shows what is standing, the rate against its target, and what is shelved.

items.lead: Acknowledge by name, with a note
items.text: The name, the moment and the note enter the record, and every open screen shows it at once.
The live value, the half hour before it against its limit, and the cause, the consequence and the action the engineer wrote.
One entry per alarm carrying that reason, and the most critical band held back to be answered one at a time.

items.lead: Shelve with a reason and a return time
items.text: A nuisance alarm leaves the board for a bounded time, everyone sees why and until when, and it comes back by itself.
The response times, the flood episodes and the alarms that raise most — the insights ISA-18.2 and EEMUA 191 ask for.

items.lead: A journal that survives the rule
items.text: Switch a rule off, repoint or delete it, and every alarm it raised stays in the journal, each saying why it ended.
What was still standing and still unanswered at the boundary, with the outgoing supervisor's note and signature.

items.lead: View in TimeLens from an alarm
items.text: One press from the alarm to that page at that moment.

screens.caption: the alarm on its own card: the live value, the half hour against its limit, the guidance — and View in TimeLens
the rules behind it: the editor's alarm list on a real line, one row per rule

sections.title: An alarm is an event with a record.
cols: An engineer writes the rule once, the edge beside the machine judges it, and the person who answers leaves their name on the record. The board, the journal, the numbers and the printed sheet all read the same rows, so an alarm cannot mean one thing on a screen and another on paper.
The same event carries the rule that judged it, the person who answered it, the screen it belonged to and the sheet it is printed on, with no second product under any of them.
Switch a rule off, point it at another signal or delete it altogether, and every alarm it already raised stays in the journal, each one saying in its own words why it ended.

Signals stacked in lanes, or laid over one another.
The shift that actually ran that day, on the plant's clock.

The note stays on the chart with the writer's name and the time on it.
Exactly the window on screen, stamped with what drew it; a link opens the same window and the same pens.
Before a chart is built, the curve's row says the signal is live only.

items.lead: The trend designer, drawing as it is typed
items.text: The real chart draws beside the form, on real history, at the window the operator will open on.

screens.caption: a day of plant signals in lanes with the shifts behind them

sections.title: The engineer draws the chart. The operator finishes it.
cols: A trend is a saved chart: the signals an engineer chose, the window it opens on, and how the bands are laid out. In the control room it stops being a picture and becomes an instrument, because the operator can add the curve nobody planned for and keep it for the next shift.
A curve you add is yours alone, and nothing you do on the chart changes what anyone else opens.
It is the same database the screen is already drawing from, and every operator already has it.

sections.title: Historian
The history is part of the platform, not a product beside it.

screen.chrome: the editor · Beverage Line 7 · the trend designer
screen.caption: the chart being built, drawing as it is typed, on real history

items.lead: The plant and its history, one box
items.text: The plant and its history stand on the same box, never two systems to reconcile.

items.lead: Not a product beside the SCADA
items.text: In the class the history chart is a product beside the SCADA, with its own licence and its own seat; here it is the same database the screen is already drawing from, and every operator already has it.
Averages are count-weighted, never an average of averages.

items.lead: A quality byte on every reading
items.text: A quality byte rides every reading, so a number the plant should not trust says so.
Correct a value from years ago and every total since corrects itself — there is no second copy to migrate.

items.lead: Any window, and it names the resolution
items.text: A month of a slow signal draws as fast as a short window, and the chart names the resolution it answered from.
Cut the network and the readings wait on the edge's own disk, then fill the gap in.
One key follows a signal from the controller's register to the pixel, the trend, the batch, the work order and the printed sheet.

items.lead: The history is inside the licence
items.text: The database and the historian are what the licence already contains, with every project drawn, duplicated and exported.

sections.title: One database. One history.
cols: One database, Postgres; one historian beside it, TimescaleDB; the plant and its history on the same box — dozens of lines, every reading, on two servers. Nothing in the stack is sunsetting.
Ask for a month of a slow signal and it draws as fast as a short window — and the chart names the resolution it used.
Nothing is mapped a second time. One key follows a signal from the register to the pixel, the trend, the batch, the work order and the printed sheet.

Each sees the other is there, and a stale save is refused rather than quietly merged.
A curated library by equipment family, each body drawn to process scale and carrying the failure words the maintenance record picks from.
The engineer declutters for himself without taking anything off the operator's page.

Every binding, target and attached document follows, with fresh identities.

items.lead: The line as one portable file
items.text: Export it, import it at the next plant: names travel and identities do not, so nothing can collide with what is already there.

sections.title: The engineer builds against the running line.
cols: Engineers draw in a browser, and nothing is licensed per workstation. A finished line is copied in one press and carried to the next plant as a single portable file.
A banner says who else is on the page, and it never blocks anyone. A save made against a page that has moved on is refused rather than quietly merged.
The eye hides a layer for the engineer alone; the operator's page keeps everything until a switch or a plant condition takes it off.

The page designer has two modes, and the second one is the operator's own screen. The rest of the editor works the same way: the signal list, the binder and the trend all read the running line while the work is still being done.
No restart, no simulation: the reading above is the real one.
Preview dresses the buttons for the role you choose, and the database still judges the person signed in.

sections.title: Two lenses: one over time, one over the tags.
cols: The operator's question is what happened at a moment. The engineer's question is what a signal touches before it is changed. Each has a lens, and each answers from the one database.
Any page replays from the historian: back and forward, alarm to alarm, or straight to a moment. The replayed screen wears gold and its commands are off, so it can never be mistaken for live.
A moment link pastes into a message and a colleague opens the same second on the same screen. From an alarm row, one press lands on the screen as it was when the alarm raised.

sections.title: One signal, followed through every module.
cols: We know of no other platform that follows one tag through every module of the plant. A migration is a thousand signals moved; here each one shows what it touches before it is touched.
The engineer's question is what a signal touches before it is changed — and it is answered from the one database, not from a spreadsheet of bindings.

The edge runs the line. The server only receives.

items.lead: The edge that holds the line
items.text: One executable beside the controller polls the devices, judges the alarms, holds the history and writes the operator's commands back.
SOP supports all major drivers — Modbus, OPC DA, Siemens S7 and OPC UA among them.
Cut the network and the readings wait on the edge's own disk, then fill the gap in.

items.lead: A second edge on the same devices
items.text: Where a line cannot afford to lose its edge, a second one stands on the same devices and takes over.

items.lead: The server, on the substrate you choose
items.text: From scripts, in a single session, on plain hardware in your own plant, air gapped if your rules say so, or on a cloud backbone; the plant and its history on the same box.

items.lead: Duty and standby, one address that moves
items.text: Two identical servers, one address the plant dials; a planned handover refuses unless both are in step, and a standby that cannot see the plant stands down. The standby is part of the platform, not a second purchase.

items.lead: Two servers for the whole plant
items.text: Not a standby bought for every engine: one duty, one standby, one address, for every line and every edge.

items.lead: The plant's own pages, served by the edge
items.text: If the server cannot be reached, the edge serves the pages the operators trained on: the same drawing, the same symbols, the same commands, live values and standing alarms.

items.lead: It refuses a login while the server is healthy
items.text: The emergency access opens only while the server is unreachable, and closes when it returns.

sections.title: Availability is the architecture, not an option.
cols: One executable sits beside the controller and does the work the line depends on: it polls the devices, judges the alarms, holds the history and writes the operator's commands back. The server in the middle only receives, which is why a server that stops is an inconvenience and never an outage.
A server that stops loses no plant data: it never lived only there. One store, nothing to reconcile. Adding a way to stay up costs a setting, not a licence.

The emergency HMI — we know of no other platform that does this. If both servers are unreachable, the operators keep running the plant from the edge itself: no extra HMI panel, no second application — the same SCADA pages the server designed are already stored on the edge, and the edge serves them directly, with the same symbols, the same commands, live values and standing alarms, until the centre is back.
Not one of these four changes a screen anybody uses: the edge buffers on every install, and the pair and the emergency password are set once by the administrator.

sections.title: Rights and the record
What a user may not see never reaches them.

screen.chrome: the console · the fleet · the audit journal
screen.caption: the audit journal across the whole fleet, in four lenses, filtered and exported

items.lead: Rights in one console, read in the database
items.text: A screen a person may not open is never sent to their browser, their export or their sheet.
Six rungs: the licence · the switch · the role and the scope · the group · the list · the record.
A contractor runs one line and nothing else; the press is refused in the database anywhere else, not merely greyed out on the screen.
One list to keep, and a new starter is covered the day they join it.

items.lead: Can see and open, per page
items.text: The pages leave everyone else's tree, in the control room and on the phone; off the list a page goes away, not grey.
Everybody keeps watching the valve, and nobody else can move it.
The module leaves everyone else's menu on that line, and stays as it was on the others.
The next sign in is refused, and the record of what they did stays.

items.lead: The licence and the module switch
items.text: A module nobody bought never appears, and a line it is off on never shows it.
Every command, acknowledgement, shelving and grant across the fleet, each with its moment, in four lenses, narrowed and exported.

sections.title: What a user may not see never reaches them.
cols: Rights are set in one console and decided in the database, so a screen a person may not open is never sent to their browser, their export or their sheet. The same console reaches from a whole site down to one screen, one signal and one module, and it keeps the record of every act that follows.

Off a list a page does not go grey for other people, it goes away: it leaves the operator's page browser, it leaves the editor's tree, and every button that led to it goes with it. A global administrator is the one who can hand it back.

A right set in a client menu can only withhold the drawing, because the data has already travelled. Here the rule that hides a screen is the same rule that filters the export and the printed sheet, because there is one database under all three: what a person may not see is never sent.
And the record the auditor reads is the screen's own rows: the numbers on the sheet are the same rows the operator was watching, so the tile and the paper cannot disagree.
